title: Field friction and win paths: LLM endpoints (ops-focused)
body:
Purpose
This note is an ops-first field brief: short scripts, risk-based differentiators, and friction maps for sales/SEs confronting generic LLM API vendors. Goal: win deals where customers list reliability, predictability, or regulatory constraints as buying signals.

TL;DR (elevator)
- Customers care about predictable p99 latency, predictable unit economics, and graceful degradation under load. Redwood wins when we frame inference as a systems problem (serving + routing + cache) rather than a model-only feature.
- Top play: anchor on SLOs + fallbacks + clear economic levers (batching, caching, quantization) and close with a small pilot that proves tail latency under real traffic.

Primary personas and motivations
- Platform/Infrastructure Lead (SRE/Platform): cares about SLOs, operational visibility, and escape hatches. Wants rollout controls, tracing, and way to enforce quotas.
- ML Engineer / Model Ops: cares about model accuracy vs quantization, deterministic rollbacks, canary testing. Wants kernel-level performance and KV cache controls.
- Product/PM (consumer-facing): cares about UX (streaming, token costs), predictable billing, and compliance.

Trigger events we target for outreach
- Existing provider had an incident (multi-hour outage or severe tail latency spike).
- Rapid traffic increase (marketing campaign or new feature) that makes costs explode.
- Regulated workloads that need VPC/on-prem or KMS integration.

Core positioning points (ops lane)
- Production-grade SLOs: we offer documented latency/availability SLOs with canary/fallback policies built into the platform.
- Deterministic fallbacks: traffic can automatically shift to quantized or cheaper model variants with no client-side changes.
- Unit economics transparency: token-level cost breakdown + concrete knobs you can toggle (e.g., batch size, aggressive prefix caching).
- Observable serving runtime: per-request tracing (route, kernel selection, cache hit/miss) + token latency breakdowns for troubleshooting.

Competitor shorthand (quick call cheat-sheet)
- Generic LLM API provider A (large cloud incumbent): great model breadth, weak on enterprise fallbacks and custom routing. Weak spot: no private VPC option and limited traceability for tail latency.
- LLM-specialist B (simplicity-first): very easy to get started, but single execution path and brittle under bursty traffic. Weak spot: one-size kernel, no quantization profiles, high unit cost at scale.
- Open-source-stack integrator C (self-host tools): flexible and cheap but requires heavy ops work and lacks SLA, rollouts, and integrated billing/usage analytics. Weak spot: hidden integration costs and long time-to-prod.

Opportunities to exploit (friction map)
- If customer says “we can just switch models to save money” -> counter: switching models without a serving layer causes unpredictable latency and regressions; Redwood’s routing + evals reduce regression risk.
- If competitor touts model accuracy only -> counter: accuracy is necessary but not sufficient; model rollout + traceability + fallback policies are what keep user-facing apps online.

Top objections and short rebuttals
- Objection: "We get cheaper tokens elsewhere."
  Rebuttal: "Token price alone doesn’t reflect total cost. We measure per-request latency cost, SRE time, and regression risk. Customers typically save on ops+token costs once batching, cache, and quantization are applied."
- Objection: "We already have an internal stack (self-host)."
  Rebuttal: "If you want control, great — Redwood Private matches that control while minimizing the integration effort. Many teams underestimate the operational burden of custom fallbacks and live rollbacks."
- Objection: "Your fallback models will be lower quality."
  Rebuttal: "We recommend graded variants that preserve critical output quality for your use-cases. We ship tooling to evaluate semantic regressions per prompt slice before enabling fallbacks."

Leverage points (scripts for SEs)
1) Discovery script (3-minute): "Tell me about your worst incident in the last 6 months related to model endpoints — what was the user impact and how did you rollback?"
   - Follow ups: "How long did debugging take? Any unknowns in the stack? Who owns the rollback?"
2) Value demo script (10-minute): "We’ll run a short replay of real traffic to show p99 tail under three configs: default, cached, and cached+quantized. We’ll surface per-token latency and economic delta in the console."
3) Contract close script: "For a 6-week pilot we’ll provision a dedicated pool, set two SLOs (p50/p99), and instrument a small prompt corpus for regression alerts — if we miss our SLO we’ll commit to an escalation and walkthrough."

Risk & trap cards (how competitors try to mislead)
- Trap: Competitor emphasizes model-centric bench results (tokens/sec on unattended benchmark).
  Response: Ask for a real production benchmark on your traffic shape (mixed seq lengths, prefix reuse). Offer to run the replays — our runtime optimizations matter most for production distribution.
- Trap: Competitor promises unlimited failover with no performance caveats.
  Response: Clarify whether that means falling back to a different model family or a quantized variant. Push for a concrete RPO/RTO and discuss the quality delta and telemetry during fallback events.

Technical backup bullets for SEs
- Kernel selection: our runtime chooses kernels per-layer based on sequence length and hardware to minimize memory stalls.
- KV/prefix caching: we support automatic prefix caching and customer-granular cache policies (TTL, shard keys).
- Quantization profiles: recommend per-model profiles (int8 vs int4) and show historical eval deltas on representative prompt slices.

Pricing framing (simple)
- Avoid token-only conversations. Offer a unit-economics memo: (token cost) + (ops overhead per seat) + (SLO provisioning surcharge for dedicated pools).
- Pilot offer: 30 days of discounted reserved capacity for production-like traffic replay, with telemetry export and a cost optimization post-mortem.

Demo / pilot checklist (SE playbook)
- Get prompt corpus (10–50 representative prompts) and a replay window (3–6 hours)
- Provision dedicated test pool with routing rules and fallback policies
- Enable trace sampling and token-level latency metrics
- Run default -> enable prefix cache -> enable quantized variant while measuring quality regression
- Deliver one-pager with p50/p99 and cost delta, plus recommended rollout plan

Collateral to attach to outbound or pitch doc
- Short one-pager: "SLO-first inference: what to expect in week 0–6" (include p50/p99 language, fallback story)
- Technical appendix: kernel selection and cache architecture (2 pages)
- Case vignette: "Retail client reduced p99 by 3x with prefix caching + fallback" (anonymized)

Open questions / assumptions to validate with engineering
- What is the minimum traffic shape we can realistically simulate for a meaningful p99 test? (A: need 1000–10k requests with taily distribution; confirm with runtime team)
- Can we pre-package a sample quantization profile for common open models to shorten pilot time?

Next actions (owner + timeline)
- Maya: draft the pilot one-pager and a pilot pricing template (due 2025-10-09).
- Ava: validate minimal traffic replay size with serving-runtime (due 2025-10-03).
- Ravi: prepare two canned eval suites for quantization regression (due 2025-10-06).

Notes to self / scratch items
- Keep scripts short and tactile; ops leads want checklists not big slides.
- Example Slack snippet for AE to use after outage discovery: "Sorry to hear about the incident — can we run a 1-hour traffic replay next week to show how routing/fallbacks behave under your traffic shape?"

Quick links (for the SE)
- Internal replay runbook: CONFLUENCE-REPLAY-RUNBOOK
- Pilot pricing template: JIRA-SALES-PRICING-77
- Eval runner PR: github.com/redwood-inference/response-quality-evals/pull/98

End.
